messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I hope this email finds you well.

In traditional SEM, mediation models are straightforward and well-documented (for reference, see the lavaan tutorial: https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html).

Given my smaller sample size (N = 686), I’m exploring the possibility of running my mediation analysis within the Structural After Measurement (SAM) approach instead. However, I’m currently seeking guidance on how to adapt or implement a mediation model using the SAM methodology.

Here is my hypothesis (adapted from SEM):
Ant ~ a1 * ACE
Dis ~ a2 * ACE
ASB ~ b1 * Ant
ASB ~ b2 * Dis
ind1 := a1 * b1
ind2 := a2 * b2

Where:
Ant = Antagonism
Dis = Disinhibition
ACE = Adverse Childhood Experiences
ASB = Antisocial Behavior

If you’ve worked on something similar or have insights/resources for implementing a mediation model using SAM, I would greatly appreciate your advice or recommendations!

Thank you in advance for your time and support.

Best regards,
Maximilian

messages.body_plain:
Hello there,
I am trying to build an SEM to understand the causal relationship between a bunch of environmental variables and "stability" in a landscape. Stability has been calculated using trend analyses of an vegetation index. The environmental variables consist of climatic variables, heterogeneity of the area, percentage of area that burned due to fire, distance of area to the closest anthropic land use (proxy for anthropic land use pressures) and water table depth. First, I drew all the relationships plainly in Powerpoint, see image below.
I want to construct two composite variables- background climate conditions from two indicators of long term seasonality and long term annual temperature and climate pulse stressors from two indicators of drought and heatwaves. I followed the advice from this post  <https://www.r-bloggers.com/2011/05/ecological-sems-and-composite-variables-what-why-and-how/>and this post <https://jslefche.github.io/sem_book/composite-variables.html#grace-keeley-revisited-a-worked-example> about how to set the composite variables. Note the two links are different blogposts/resources about setting composite variables.

My model is

comp_trial1<- '
  #Climate composite variables
  backgroundclimate_composite <~ 1*longterm_rainfallseasonality + mean_annual_temp
  backgroundclimate_composite ~~ 0*backgroundclimate_composite
  pulse_stressors <~ 1*droughtindex + heatwave
  pulse_stressors ~~ 0*pulse_stressors

 #regression
 stable_area ~ 1*backgroundclimate_composite + 1*pulse_stressors + water_depth +    pixel_hetero +  anthropic_dist + burnedarea
  ndvi_stability ~~ 1*ndvi_stability

 #remaining relationships
  pulse_stressors ~ backgroundclimate_composite
  biodiversity ~ pulse_stressors + backgroundclimate_composite + anthropic_dist
  burnedarea ~ pulse_stressors + backgroundclimate_composite
  heatwave ~~ mat #covariance correlated
'
Using this post from this google grou <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/-e9DNa_1MPE>p, in the main regression formula I set the loadings of the two climate composite variables as equal to each other (and equal to 1). If I plainly only include the two climate composites without equal loading, then the lavaan model fails. First question- why is the model failing and why do I need to use equal loading?

So my sample size is 3700 and all data are continuous and non- normal, see plot of  distributions and correlations between variables below

Also note that since the units of all variables are not comparable, I scaled the data to be centered around the mean of each variable. Considering the non-normal distributions, I run the sem model using bootstrapping using the Satorra Bentler test

    modeltrial1<- sem(comp_trial1, scaled_analyses_ndvistability, se= "boot", test =   "Satorra.Bentler", bootstrap = 1000, fixed.x= F)
    summary(modeltrial1, standardize = T, fit.measures = TRUE)

The model runs but the model fit statistics are really bad, see result image below. Second question- what is wrong with my model such that the test statistics of corrected Chi sq, CFI, TLI and RMSEA are so bad? How do I improve my model fitness?

Looking at the model fitness statistics above, I have not even checked if the coefficients and the rest of the results make sense. Please help.

messages.subject: Re: SAM fit indices interpretation
messages.body_plain:
On 2/5/25 4:49 AM, Gairan Pamei wrote:
> I ran local SAM and for the structural part, the fit indices are found
> to be:
> chisq df cfi rmsea srmr 0 0 1 0 0
> Does not this indicate a perfect fit? This seems suspicious, too good to
> be true.

This is perfectly normal. It simply indicates that the structural part
of your model is saturated. This is not a bad thing per se. It just
means there is no way to 'test' the structural model. But you can still
interpret the coefficients. (BTW: all regression models are saturated).

> Also, is there a reason/a possibility to ignore the fit indices in SAM
> and focus on the  coefficients (e.g., of the regression or paths)?

Only when the (structural) part is saturated. Otherwise, you should
report the fit indices.

In addition, I would also report the chi-square values (and degrees of
freedom) of the measurement blocks.

Yves.

This indeed not trivial when data is categorical. This is due to the
fact that 'newdata' is processed just like the original data, and then
we check if newdata set has the same properties as the original data.
For categorical data, this also implies we need the same number of
categories for all categorical variables.

Instead of providing a single 'not-in-sample' profile, you should add
many more, so that for each variable, all possible categories occur at
least one.

A simple trick that I use is to copy the full dataset (or a big chunk of
it), and just add the 'not-in-sample' profile to the end. And then use
this augmented dataset as the 'newdata' data.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Composite models in SEM lavaan for non-normal data
messages.body_plain:
Long story short: the current version of lavaan (or any SEM software for
that matter) does a poor job handling composites. We rely on a 'trick'
where a phantom latent variable is created, which is then the dependent
variable predicted by composite indicators. That is also why strange
tricks (like the equality constraint) are needed.

I would recommend to have a look at the cSEM package, which was designed
to handle composites, and uses various PLS-style estimation methods.

If you are brave, you can try out the github version of lavaan (0.6-20).
In this version, we have 'native' support for composites (without
tricks). The model syntax is the same, but (for now) you need the
following options to run it:

fit <- sem(yourmodel, data = yourdata, optim.gradient = "numerical",
composites = TRUE)

but this may change in the next weeks. No support for robust test
statistics yet though. In other words, this is work in progress, but you
can write your model simply as:

  #Climate composite variables
   backgroundclimate_composite <~ longterm_rainfallseasonality +
mean_annual_temp
   pulse_stressors <~ droughtindex + heatwave

  #regression
  stable_area ~ backgroundclimate_composite + pulse_stressors +

water_depth +  pixel_hetero +  anthropic_dist + burnedarea

  #remaining relationships
   pulse_stressors ~ backgroundclimate_composite
   biodiversity ~ pulse_stressors + backgroundclimate_composite +
anthropic_dist
   burnedarea ~ pulse_stressors + backgroundclimate_composite
   heatwave ~~ mat #covariance correlated

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Can we assume that Ant/Dis/ACE/ASB are latent variables measured by
indicators?

In that case, there is no difference between SEM and SAM when it comes
to mediation analysis. The syntax is the same.

If you have two groups, then you should vectorize your labels. So
instead of

Ant ~ a1 * ACE

you should write

Ant ~ c(a1.g1, a1.g2) * ACE

where 'g1' and 'g2' stands for the first and second group respectively.
Then, in a follow up model, you can replace this by

Ant ~ c(a1, a1) * ACE

where you use the same label for both groups. Then you will constrain
this coefficient to be same across the groups.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On 2/5/25 2:18 PM, Tatiana Marci wrote:
> I am estimating a latent change score model and encountered an issue
> when including sex as a covariate

If sex is binary (say 0/1), and you treat it as a random variable,
lavaan will try to estimate both the mean and the variance. But they are
linked, so one of them is redundant.

One possibility would be to impose a constraint like this:

sex ~ p*1     # mean
sex ~~ q*sex  # variance

q == p * (p - 1) # constraint

Alternatively, if sex is exogenous in the model, you can use fixed.x =
TRUE (which is the default).

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Best way to report indirect effects in a complex Structural Equation Model (SEM) with a large number of variables and paths
messages.subject_clean: Best way to report indirect effects in a complex Structural Equation Model (SEM) with a large number of variables and paths
messages.body_plain:
Hello and thank you all for your reviews which helped me to find out the pros and cons.

After many attempts, I have decided to show all direct, indirect, and total standardized effects in one figure. I think this gives the reader all the information they need to understand the results of the SEM.

For interested readers, here is an R code to do this, with only one indirect effect. For the full complex SEM model described above, the R code and data will be made available at OSF <https://osf.io/jr5b6/>.

I use the built-in PoliticalDemocracy dataset.

    # Fit a SEM model
    library(lavaan)

    model <- '
    # measurement model
      ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
      dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
      dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

    # regressions
      # direct effect
        dem65 ~ c*ind60

      # mediator
        dem60 ~ a*ind60
        dem65 ~ b*dem60

      # indirect effect (a*b)
        ind60_dem60_dem65 := a*b

      # total effect
        total := c + (a*b)
    '

    fit_model <- sem(model, PoliticalDemocracy)

Here is the code to plot the effects

    # Plot the standardized direct and indirect effects
    library(tidyverse)
    library(semTools)

    monteCarloCI(fit_model, standardized = TRUE) %>%
      rownames_to_column(var = "Indirect_Paths") %>%
      mutate(Indirect_Paths = case_when(
        Indirect_Paths == "ind60_dem60_dem65" ~ "Ind in 1960 → Dem in 1960 → Dem in 1965",
        Indirect_Paths == "total" ~ "Ind in 1960 → Dem in 1965
    (Total effect)")) %>%
      bind_rows( # Get the direct effect from standardizedsolution(fit_model, ci = T)
        tibble(
          Indirect_Paths = "Ind in 1960 → Dem in 1965
    (Direct effect)",
          est.std = 0.146,
          ci.lower = 0.008,
          ci.upper = 0.283
        )
      ) %>%

      ggplot(aes(x = Indirect_Paths, y = est.std)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey", size = 0.5, alpha = 0.8) +
      geom_point(size = 0.5) +
      geom_errorbar(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.3,
                    aes(ymin = ci.lower, ymax = ci.upper),
                    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
                    width = 0.25) +
      coord_flip() +
      geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(round(ci.lower, 3) * round(ci.upper, 3) > 0, glue::glue("{round(est.std, 2)}*"), glue::glue("{round(est.std, 2)}"))),
                size = 2.5, vjust = -1.5) +
      theme_minimal() +
      labs(x = "Path",
           y = "Standardized estimate",
           caption = "Direct effect 95% confidence intervals calculated with the Delta method.
           Indirect and total effects 95% confidence intervals calculated from 9,999 Monte-Carlo repetitions.
           * Asterisks indicate that the 95% confidence interval does not include zero at the three-digits level.") +
      theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6),
            axis.title.y = element_text(size = 8),

            axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6),
            axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8),
            plot.caption = element_text(size = 5, face = "italic")) +
      expand_limits(y = c(-0.1))

    # Export the plot
    ggplot2::ggsave("Plot.jpeg", height = 3, width = 4)

This will give you the attached plot.

messages.body_plain:
Yves--
     To live in such times...SmartPLS adds CFA capability and lavaan is going to include the modeling of composites.
     I have found that the Hensler-Ogasawara (H-O) specification works pretty well. With p observed variables loading on a common factor, you replace the p observed variable residual terms with p - 1 terms. Now the number of observed and unobserved terms is the same, and you are modeling a composite, not a common factor. In simulations, at population level, H-O produces results identical to those for PLS Mode B and GSCA's form with weights only (both use regression weights rather than the correlation weights of PLS Mode A and GSCA with weights and loadings). The H-O specification would be really easy to automate, since it just involves specific patterns of loadings fixed to 1 or 0, or free, and fixed covariances. The method also works for modeling one group of observed variables as a composite while leaving other groups of observed variables loading on common factors.
     I'm attaching some slides which are a subset of a presentation I made at the American Psychological Association convention in August, in Seattle. The whole deck plus syntax (using lavaan) are posted at osf.io--see the QR code on the first slide.
     Joerg Henseler and colleagues say they have made further learnings in terms of optimal starting values. It looks pretty straightforward to me, at this point, and easily automated.
--Ed Rigdon

Dear Yves,

Thank you very much for your helpful feedback! I’m sorry for not providing enough details earlier. To clarify, the variables I mentioned are all latent variables measured by indicators and at first I fitted each measurement model.

I followed your recommendations, and everything worked well — thank you again! I now have a couple of follow-up questions as I continue analyzing my results:

Global vs. Local SAM Fit Indices
I used the global SAM method to obtain pseudo-fit indices, as I understood this is the appropriate approach (hopefully, I interpreted it correctly!). When using the global SAM method, the fit indices across groups don’t differ much, which seems reasonable.

However, I noticed that the fit indices from the local SAM method differ significantly compared to the global SAM fit indices. Do you know why this might be the case? Is it expected for global and local SAM to produce such different results?

Constraining the Model Across Groups
Did I understand correctly that you would recommend not constraining the model across groups using e.g. group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts", "regressions")?

Interaction Effects Between Groups and Predictors
Even if the fit indices are comparable between the models, regression coefficients differ between the groups.
Would you recommend explicitly testing for an interaction effect between group membership and the predictor variable? Or would this interaction essentially lead us back to the same group-specific effects already identified in the model?

I appreciate your patience and guidance as I work through these questions. Thank you again for your help!

Best regards,
Maximilian

>
> If you have two groups, then you should vectorize your labels. So
> instead of
>

>
> you should write
>

>
> Ant ~ c(a1, a1) * ACE
>
> where you use the same label for both groups. Then you will constrain
> this coefficient to be same across the groups.
>
> Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Miljan.

When you set std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, you are saying that the latent variables have all mean = 0 and variance = 1, what is not true in your population model.
However, in your case, it is not true because ATT and INT are endogenous variables, do your population variance is the residual variance, and I am not sure whether simsem/lavaan understand the difference between total and residual variance when you use std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE . My guess is that they don’t.

So, I believe you’ll need to write the population model using unstandardized coefficients — i.e., the identification of the model will be done by fixing the first factor loading of each factor to 1. Or you’ll have to compute the power for these parameters manually using simsem output.

Best,
Yago

Hello,
Please, I need urgent help with the moderated mediation analysis I am conducting. I have included the codes below. Predictors are latent variables, mediator is continuous, moderator and outcome variables  are binary (0/1).
First, I did the mediation analysis:
modermd < - "
gnts=~ dis1 + dis2 + dis3 + dis4 +dis4+dis6
knts =~ pub1 + pub2 + pub3
Ints  =~ img1 + img2 + img3
  #mediation
  totdp ~ a1*gnts+ a2*knts+ a3*Ints
  #outcomes
  TRT_Ad ~c1*gnts+ c2*knts+ c3*Ints
  + b1*totdp + age
 #Indirect effects
  a1b1 := a1*b1
  a2b1 := a2*b1
  a3b1 := a3*b1
#Total effects
c1a1 := c1 + a1b1
  c2a2 := c2 + a2b1
  c3a3 := c3 + a3b1
"
TRT_FIT = sem(modermd, data = ADH_analtbl,
              ordered = "TRT_Ad ",
              estimator = "DWLS")
summary(TRT_FIT, fit.measures = T)
bootfit_fit<- sem(modermd, data = ADH_analtbl,
                    ordered = "TRT_Ad ",
                    se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 5000, estimator = "DWLS",
                    verbose = TRUE)
parameterEstimates(bootfit_fit, boot.ci.type = "bca.simple", standardized = TRUE, ci=TRUE)

I included it as a numeric variable since Lavaan does not permit including it as a factor in the analysis. Given that the predictor is a latent variable, I utilized the indprod function from the semTools package to create the interaction terms needed for the moderated mediation analyses, as outlined below:

df_moderated <- indProd(ADH_analtbl, var1 =1img1:img3, var2 = provt, match=F, residualC = T)

Hi Sandra,

the first step is to test for invariance (equivalence). If you only want to compare the regression coefficients, you should at least test for configural and metric invariance. If you are also interested in mean differences, it would also make sense to test for scalar invariance. There are various approaches for this. I personally like this one: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29172611/

In this very simple example (which does not exactly correspond to your model), the moderator is tested using a self-defined parameter:

library(lavaan)

# Simulate some data
pop.model.g1 <- "
IV =~ 1 * x1 + 1 * x2 + 1 * x3
DV =~ 1 * y1 + 1 * y2 + 1 * y3
DV ~ 0.2 * IV"

pop.model.g2 <- "
IV =~ 1 * x1 + 1 * x2 + 1 * x3
DV =~ 1 * y1 + 1 * y2 + 1 * y3
DV ~ 0.6 * IV"

n <- c(100, 100)
data <- cbind(
  group = c(rep(1, n[1]), rep(2, n[2])),
  rbind(
    simulateData(pop.model.g1, sample.nobs = n[1], empirical = TRUE),
    simulateData(pop.model.g2, sample.nobs = n[2], empirical = TRUE)
  )
)

# Specify the model
model <- "
IV =~ x1 + x2 + x3
DV =~ y1 + y2 + y3
DV ~ c(b.g1,b.g2) * IV
mod := b.g2 - b.g1
"

fit <- sem(model, data, group = "group", group.equal = "loadings")
parameterEstimates(fit)

Christian

Dear all,

I'm a nature science student, very new to SEM and lavaan, and I really need your help to evaluate the soundness of my methodology. In my study, I use path analysis to study carnivore-farmers conflicts in Eastern Honduras. My goal is to integrate the path analysis into a Causal Loop Diagram explaining socioeconomic implications in the shaping of stakeholders perceptions towards carnivores.

The sample size is rather small: 104 observations. In my model, I include variables of different type, and with different levels, and this is the main challenge.

Exogenous Variables:

Residency time: continuous
Education level: ordinal, 4 levels: 1,2,3,4
Age: continuous
Ethnicity: binary (indigenous, non-indigenous)

Endogenous Variables:

a) Moderators
Adaptive Husbandry: binary (yes, no)
Acknowledgement Benefits: ordinal, 3 levels: -1,0,1
Engagement in Conservation: binary (yes,no)
Awareness Ecological Value: binary (yes no
b) Outcome variables
Tolerance: binary (yes,no)
Readiness to Denounce Poaching: binary (yes,no)
Acceptability Lethal Control: ordinal/likert, 5 levels: 1,2,3,4,5

I chose to treat the ordinal variables as numeric, because of the small sample size, using therefore Maximum Likelihood as estimator. I then studied the indirect effects to test the validity of the causal path. I scaled continuous variables to tackle the issue of extreme differences in variances, and used "fiml" to deal with NAs.

here is the code in lavaan:

df_tolerance$age_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$age)
df_tolerance$residency_clean_scaled <- scale(df_tolerance$residency_clean)

                engagement_in_conservation ~ b2*acknowledgement_benefits
                awareness ~ acknowledgement_benefits
                acknowledgement_benefits ~ residency_scaled + education_level
                tolerance ~ b1*adaptive_husbandry + b4*awareness
                readiness_to_denounce ~ b3*engagement_in_conservation + age_scaled
                acceptability_lethal_control ~ acknowledgement_benefits + engagement_in_conservation

IE_residency_tolerance := a1*b1

IE_age_tolerance := a3*b1

IE_residency_lethal := a1*b2
IE_education_tolerance := a4*b1
IE_education_tolerance2 := a4*b2*b4
IE_education_lethal := a4*b2
'

fit_joint <- sem(model_joint, data = df_tolerance, missing="fiml")
summary(fit_joint, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE)

First, that's a heck of a complex model for a pretty small sample size.

Your specific questions:

1) (Considering the sample size) Do I need to use DWSL instead of ML? Even if I have a categorical ordinal variable as exogenous? In that case, do I have to set as "ordered" binary variables too?

No, I don't think your sample is large enough. I would be surprised it it converged / was identified (although there's no harm in trying). It took 40 iterations to converge, which is a lot.

2) Is there any other thing I have to think about while validating my model that I'm missing?

Not that are obvious to me.

3) Do You have any suggestions?

Your sample is too small to draw much in the way of conclusions. You have little power to reject the model if it is wrong (and a lot of parameters with large standard errors).

Your chi-square is not significant, but that's not a huge surprise at this sample size. Your null model is not awful, hence your TLI is not particularly high. The confidence intervals on your RMSEA are pretty wide.

The path diagram is not hugely clear to me (it's also very small, I can't read it). I try to make the diagram 'flow' from left to right - it looks like you have four exgoenous variables. Start with those four on the left, then these all have arrows pointing to the next two variables, etc.

Hope that helps (and wasn't too harsh),

Jeremy

It is a triangular system (the arrows flow in a specific direction, so you can write it up with demographics on top, and acceptability on the bottom, and the matrix of the coefficients to be estimated will be lower triangular). I'd say it should be estimated as an econometric simultaneous equations model (series of regressions), and not bother with formulating it as a latent variable model (which is what lavaan really expects). My understanding is that lavaan recognizes demographics as exogenous variables here, but since you asked for FIML, it still tries too hard to fit the model that is too reliant on multivariate normality. The reference I was able to find is https://bookdown.org/ccolonescu/RPoE4/simultaneous-equations-models.html (except of course rm(list=ls()) for which the author's computer should be burned, per Jenny Bryan's guidance).

Hi Toby,

I'm not entirely sure if I understand your question correctly, so please take my answer with a grain of salt.

For a two group model, the mean difference of the latent variable (Y) is, in principle, identical to the result of a regression where the group variable (X or group, as you label it) serves as the IV and the latent variable (Y) as the DV. Differences may occur under certain circumstances, depending on the level of invariance.

Suppose you have another latent variable (M) that acts as a mediator between the group variable and Y. You can interpret the multi-group model as follows:

(1) The mean difference of M corresponds to the direct effect of X (group) on M.
(2) The direct effect of X (group) on Y is the mean difference of Y.
(3) The direct effect of M on Y is part of the model.

Accordingly, you can determine the indirect and total effect of X on Y as in a typical mediator model (with X as an exogenous variable). Does this roughly answer your question?

Here is a small example (hopefully without typos):

library(lavaan)

# Simulate some data
pop.model.g1 <- "

M =~ 1 * x1 + 1 * x2 + 1 * x3
Y =~ 1 * y1 + 1 * y2 + 1 * y3
Y ~ 0.4 * M"

pop.model.g2 <- "
M =~ 1 * x1 + 1 * x2 + 1 * x3
Y =~ 1 * y1 + 1 * y2 + 1 * y3
Y ~ 0.4 * M
M ~ 0.3 * 1
Y ~ 0.5 * 1"

n <- c(100, 100)
data <- cbind(
  group = c(rep(1, n[1]), rep(2, n[2])),
  rbind(
    simulateData(pop.model.g1, sample.nobs = n[1], empirical = TRUE),
    simulateData(pop.model.g2, sample.nobs = n[2], empirical = TRUE)
  )
)

# Regression
model <- "
Y =~ y1 + y2 + y3
Y ~ group"
fit <- sem(model, data)
pe <- parameterEstimates(fit)
pe[pe$op == "~",]

# Mean difference
model <- "
Y =~ y1 + y2 + y3
Y~ c(0, NA) * 1"
fit <- sem(model, data, group = "group", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
pe <- parameterEstimates(fit)
pe[pe$op == "~1",]

# Same for mediation
model <- "
M =~ x1 + x2 + x3
Y =~ y1 + y2 + y3
M ~ a * group
Y ~ b * M + c * group
ind := a * b
tot := ind + c"

fit <- sem(model, data)
pe <- parameterEstimates(fit)
pe[pe$op %in% c("~", ":="),]

# MG approach
model <- "
M =~ x1 + x2 + x3
Y =~ y1 + y2 + y3
M ~ c(m.0, a) * 1
Y ~ b * M
Y ~ c(m.0, c) * 1
m.0 == 0
ind := a * b
tot := ind + c"

fit <- sem(model, data, group = "group", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
pe <- parameterEstimates(fit)
pe[pe$op %in% c("~", "~1", ":="),]
